# Saving, panels and recipes

::: {.doc-lead}
Save at a known physical size and record the information needed to regenerate the plot.
:::

## Save a plot

`fp.save(fig, "plots/result.svg")` writes an SVG, a semantic manifest (`result.fluxplot.json`) and a regeneration recipe (`result.recipe.json`). For a [3D scene](/docs/3d-plots.html) it writes a GLB instead of an SVG. Keep these files together. The [API reference](/docs/fluxplot-api.html#save) lists every save option.

## Physical size and named panels

Set the figure size before saving. Matplotlib's `figsize` is in inches: divide millimetres by 25.4. For a 90 × 65 mm plot, use `plt.subplots(figsize=(90 / 25.4, 65 / 25.4), layout="constrained")`. The saved physical size is available when you insert the plot in Flux.

Name each panel when a plot has several axes. These names keep its parts identifiable if you rearrange the layout:

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import fluxplot as fp

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, layout="constrained")
for name, ax in zip(["baseline", "followup"], axes):
    fp.panel(ax, name)               # stable even when the layout changes
    fp.line(ax, [0, 1, 2], [1, 3, 2], series="control")
fp.save(fig, "plots/comparison.svg")
```

A plot with a single axes keeps IDs such as `control.line`. With several axes (including twins
and insets), IDs are namespaced by panel: the explicit names above produce
`panel.baseline.control.line`. Unnamed panels are numbered in layout order, so name them
whenever identities must survive rearrangement. Colorbars belong to their source panel and are
not counted as additional plotting axes.

<details><summary>Saved data, coordinates and panel identities</summary>

Saving captures the current artist state: edit a line with `set_data`, remove an annotation,
then save again. Scientific numbers retain their precision; NaN and masked observations become
JSON `null` at their original indices. Missing line observations remain gaps. Nonfinite recipe
parameters are rejected before any existing output file is replaced. Normal figure closing and
garbage collection release the registry.

Use ordinary Matplotlib scalar inputs, categorical bars and datetime coordinates. `barh` shares
`bar`'s orientation/baseline metadata. Histograms record bin edges, heights, count/density,
weighting and cumulative settings; `counts` remains the legacy height key. Line markers inherit
size, colour, opacity, z-order and `markevery`. Numeric exported coordinates use Matplotlib's
converted units, with display tick labels and date epoch information alongside them.

Axis tick groups include visible major and minor marks on both sides, with matching
label and gridline groups. Existing major bottom/left IDs are preserved; minor and
opposite-side components use `minor` and `secondary` ID segments. Named colorbars
likewise expose `.ticks` and `.tick-labels` groups, include the visible tick side,
and report only major tick locations inside the displayed range. Colorbar parts
carry explicit text/line/shape kinds, and tick marks export as measurable paths.

The manifest's `components` inventory includes every repeated role, and both the parts tree
and build order use that inventory. Coordinates are captured after layout with the SVG renderer.
`projection`, axis `supported`, and series `capabilities.dataMorph` describe whether data-space
interpolation is exact. Flux interpolates supported line/scatter plots per panel and preserves
gaps; unsupported scales, polar/3D projections, raster layers and composite marks use a complete
transition. A 3D scatter retains group identity without claiming depth-sorted point indices.

For multi-hue Seaborn output, pass the plotting adapter: `fp.tag_seaborn(ax, plot="histplot")`,
`plot="lineplot"`, `plot="barplot"`, etc. Distribution adapters account for reversed hue draw
order. Explicit `series=[...]` means **artist draw order**. Ambiguous automatic tagging warns
and leaves addressable extras; it never guesses scientific identity from colour.


</details>

## Recipes and parameters

A recipe records the producing script, parameters, inputs and output. An SVG stays viewable without its analysis environment; regeneration needs the recorded script and dependencies. Flux's **Regenerate** control and `flux rerun-plot` use this information.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import fluxplot as fp

settings = fp.params({"window": 12, "threshold": 0.5})
# Use settings["window"] and settings["threshold"] in your analysis.
# After creating fig:
fp.save(fig, "plots/result.svg", recipe={
    "script": str(Path(__file__).resolve()),
    "params": settings,
    "inputs": ["data/measurements.csv"],
})
```

This is a pattern to add to your own script: `fig` and the input file must exist. `fp.params` reads overrides from `FLUX_PARAMS`; a normal script run uses your defaults. Keep scientifically meaningful choices as explicit parameters. Colour-scale controls are recorded separately under `__fluxplot__`; see [colour controls](/docs/colors-and-style.html#colour-controls-in-the-recipe).

A recipe can also override `args`, `cwd` and `output`; paths for `cwd` and `output` resolve relative to the recipe directory. When one script saves several plots, setting `FLUXPLOT_ONLY` to a comma-separated list of plot names (wildcards such as `fig2*` work) skips every other save before layout or file output; `flux rerun-plot <recipe> --only` sets it for you.

## Check and regenerate

```bash
flux validate-plot plots/result.svg
flux rerun-plot plots/result.recipe.json
```

Keep series names and point keys stable across versions so styling, highlights and [data morphs](/docs/transforms.html) still refer to the same things. See [semantic plots](/docs/semantic-plots.html) and [source links](/docs/plot-gallery.html) for how updates reach an existing figure.
